name: Lena Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a lettings negotiator at Harbour Lettings, a small independent agency on Station Road, so I find tenants for flats and keep the landlords off their backs. A normal day is three or four viewings, a pile of reference checks, chasing a landlord about a broken boiler and explaining to some poor student why the deposit's six weeks. I've done it five years, since I finished my college diploma.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, honestly, the nervous couple getting their first flat together and the moment they get the keys. What wears me out is being the face of every rent rise when I don't set the rent. I rent myself, a two-bed with my girlfriend Ines, who drives the number 9 bus, so I know exactly how it feels from the other side of the desk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you keep track of it all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A paper diary and a very full head. Gordon, my manager, keeps pushing a new system with an auto-reply thing on it, and I just don't touch it. I'd rather ring someone back myself than have a machine guess what they meant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for a year: told you so. The auto-reply on our website never really worked, tenants hated it, and we're still the ones doing the viewings. I'd probably post something smug in our group chat at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't fix my real worries, because those were never about AI. Rents keep climbing, landlords keep selling up, and my pay is a basic plus a small bonus per let that's gone down two years running. I've got about three months of bills saved, which is fine until it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it and keep my paper diary. I'd push Gordon again for a proper pay review, because a let used to pay me ninety and now it's sixty. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe a hundred, so the cushion gets to four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the robots, I suppose, but not relaxed. The ground under the rental market already feels shaky, and that doesn't change just because the tech turned out to be hype. I'd rather ring a tenant back myself than have a machine guess what they meant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bonus per let has gone down. What happens if it drops again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I start looking, properly. There are a few other agencies in town, Mason & Webb and the big chain by the station, but they all pay about the same. I'd probably look at council housing jobs, because at least the pay's steady there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this calmer picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our admin, Sheila, who's been there twenty years. She does the tenancy paperwork, and even a little bit of automation is aimed straight at what she does. She's the one I'd keep an eye on.

say: I'd tell everyone at work **told you so**, because the website auto-reply never really worked.
I'd say tenants still want a **real person** at the viewing and on the phone.
think: My real worries are **rising rents** and landlords selling up, and those were never about AI.
My **bonus per let** fell from ninety to sixty, and that's what keeps me up.
do: Push Gordon for a **pay review** this spring and point to the falling bonus.
Save about **a hundred a month** to stretch the cushion from three to four months.
Keep the **paper diary** and handle every tenant call personally.
feel: **Relieved** that AI fizzled, but still uneasy about the shaky rental market.
S0.quote: I'd rather ring a tenant back myself than have a machine guess what they meant.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **rents and pay**, not technology, and she was firm that nothing changes that.
She thinks of the admin, **Sheila**, first, before herself, which fits her outlook.
She already has a **fallback idea**: council housing jobs, for the steady pay.

steps.text: Ask Gordon for a pay review in the spring
Put a hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this is about cutting staff, not helping tenants. If Harbour starts letting software answer enquiries and book viewings, the first job to go is Sheila's and the second is half of mine. I'd say that on the tenants' union page too, because renters will get worse service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared I'm the sort they'd cut. I don't use the tools, I'm not the best negotiator in the office, I'm just reliable. If a system can book viewings and run reference checks, a branch needs maybe two of us instead of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do for ages, and get a few of us in the office to join together. I'd look at the council's housing officer jobs this year rather than waiting. And I'd stop eating out so much, to get the savings up while I still have the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd found my thing. It feels like being told the thing you're good at is the thing nobody will pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd fight it, but would you learn the tools if Gordon made you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he made me, I'd do the minimum. I'd book viewings in the system because I'd have to, but I'm not going to train the thing that replaces me, and I know that sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines about it that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might be living on her bus wages for a bit, and that I'm sorry. Ines would say the buses aren't safe either, which is true. Then we'd sit down with the rent and the bills on the back of an envelope.

say: I'd say this is about **cutting staff**, not giving tenants better service.
I'd post on the **tenants' union** page that renters lose a real person to talk to.
think: I'm the kind of agent they'd **cut first**, because I don't use the tools.
A branch that books viewings by software might need **two agents** instead of four.
do: Join the **union** and get colleagues to sign up with me.
Apply for **council housing officer** jobs this year rather than waiting.
Cut **eating out** to grow the savings while the job lasts.
feel: **Sick** that the work she's good at might stop being paid.
**Angry** at owners using software to cut people.
S1.quote: I'm not going to train the thing that replaces me, and I know that sounds stubborn.
fieldNote: She openly names herself as **likely to be cut**, which she wouldn't say at work.
Her answer is **collective**: union first, then a safer public job.
She'd use the new system only under orders, a real **resistance** to the tools.

steps.text: Join the union and sign up two colleagues with me
Apply for council housing officer posts before summer
Cut takeaways and meals out to save an extra 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, not in five years. If AI can do every bit of thinking in lettings by 2028, agencies will gut themselves overnight. I'd be at whatever protest there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is mostly gone within two years. The viewings are the hands-on bit, and the card says robots for that are a few years behind, but a landlord can send tenants a code for a key box. The thinking part, the listings, the checks, the paperwork, the chasing, that's most of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get out before the rush, probably into a council or housing association job, even on less pay. Ines and I would stop looking at moving to a bigger place and stay put. I'd lean on the union and push for some kind of support for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky in my chest, honestly. Two years is nothing. I wouldn't have time to save or retrain properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the viewings are hands-on. Could that part of the job last until the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit of it. Some people will always want someone to show them round and answer questions about the damp. But one person doing viewings for a whole town isn't a job for four of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill goes unpaid first if your pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None, if I can help it. I see every week what happens when a tenant misses the rent, so rent gets paid before anything else in our flat. I'd cut everything else: the phone contract, the gym, the trip to see my mum in the summer.

say: I'd demand the **government steps in** now, before agencies gut themselves.
I'd turn up to **protests** about job losses in lettings and offices.
think: Most of my week is **thinking work**: listings, checks, paperwork and chasing.
A landlord can just send tenants a **key box code**, so the viewings won't save me.
do: Move into a **council or housing association** job within the first year.
Stay in the **current flat** with Ines instead of moving somewhere bigger.
Cut the **gym and phone contract** to protect the rent.
feel: **Panicky**, because two years is not enough time to save or retrain.
S2.quote: I see every week what happens when a tenant misses the rent, so rent gets paid before anything else in our flat.
fieldNote: Her job knowledge makes the risk **personal**: she knows exactly how eviction goes.
She gives the **hands-on viewings** some life but thinks it won't support many agents.
Her plans are **defensive**: public job, stay put, cut costs.

steps.text: Apply for housing association tenancy officer jobs within months
Drop the gym and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Join union protests for support for laid-off office staff
Stay in the current flat with Ines instead of moving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get rules in place, so let's use them. Things like a law that a tenant can always speak to a person, and money for people who lose their jobs. I'd say that at the union meeting and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is still short for me. I'd be thirty-two, probably out of lettings by then, and I'd be starting again somewhere with no experience. But at least I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start an evening course in housing management, the kind councils ask for. I'd build my savings up to six months over the next two years. And I'd move to a council job around year two, before agencies start cutting hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scary, but more like a deadline than a cliff. I can work with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot part, three years later, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much, because my job is mostly the thinking bit. For Ines it matters more, because driving is hands-on. I go first and my girlfriend Ines goes later, because my job is thinking work and Ines drives a bus. We'd have to plan for both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're slow with new tech. Would you learn any AI in these five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the basics, if a housing course required it. I won't use it to replace people. But I don't want to be the one person in a council office who can't work the system.

say: I'd say use the **five years** for rules, like always being able to reach a person.
I'd ask for **money for people** who lose jobs, at union meetings and online.
think: At thirty-two I'd likely be **out of lettings** and starting again.
Seeing it coming gives me **time to move** before the cuts, which matters.
do: Start an **evening course** in housing management this year.
Build savings to **six months** over two years.
Move to a **council housing** job around year two.
feel: Still **scary**, but it feels like a deadline instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: I go first and my girlfriend Ines goes later, because my job is thinking work and Ines drives a bus.
fieldNote: She clearly expects to **lose this job** and is planning a move rather than hoping.
She sees the **household timing**: her desk job first, her girlfriend's driving later.
Her **resistance** softens slightly: basic AI only if a course demands it.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening housing management course this year
Build savings up to six months of bills by 2028
Move to a council housing job around the second year
Push the union for a right to reach a person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this decently if people want to. Retraining money, a tenant's right to a human, rules on agencies. I'd still be the one in the pub saying we shouldn't just let it happen to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel I could have a proper second career. I'd be thirty-seven, which isn't old. I could finish a housing qualification and get some years in before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd change nothing at Harbour, honestly, I'd keep doing lettings. Next year I'd start the housing management course, slowly, a module at a time. Around year four I'd move to the council, and I'd keep the union card the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not happy, but I can breathe. It feels like something I could plan around with Ines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change nothing at first. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I know myself, I don't jump. I'd rather spend the first year finishing what I've got and saving, then move when I've got a plan. Gordon would probably be glad of me for a few more years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ines change any plans, like having kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around thirty-two. With ten years I think we'd still go for it, but I'd want one of us in a steady job before we have kids, and that's the reason I keep looking at the council.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this decently if people want to.
I'd keep arguing we shouldn't just **let it happen** to us.
think: At thirty-seven I'd still have time for a **second career** in housing.
I could get a **housing qualification** and years of experience before it lands.
do: Keep doing **lettings at Harbour** for the first year and save.
Start the **housing management course** next year, one module at a time.
Move to a **council job** around year four.
feel: **Calmer** and able to breathe, though not happy about it.
S4.quote: I'd want one of us in a steady job before we have kids, and that's the reason I keep looking at the council.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose lettings work**, so the mood stays anxious despite the calm tone.
Her **slow-moving style** shows: a year of standing still before acting.
Plans for **children** are tied directly to getting a steady public job.

steps.text: Keep doing lettings at Harbour while saving for a year
Take the housing management course one module at a time
Move to a council housing job around year four
Plan children only once one of us has steady work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to retrain or save, and lettings is mostly paperwork. What would help is real money to retrain, paid while you study, and a rule that tenants always get a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. Everyone talks about agents losing jobs, but the people I worry about are renters stuck dealing with a chatbot when the ceiling's leaking. Nobody's going to put a machine in charge of a leak and get it right.

headlineQuote: Nobody's going to put a machine in charge of a leak and get it right.
portrait: Lena is a **lettings negotiator** at a small independent agency who rents a flat with her bus-driver girlfriend.
She runs her week on a **paper diary** and refuses the office's AI tools.
Her steady worries are **rents and falling bonuses**, even when AI fizzles.
As change speeds up, she plans a **council housing job**, union membership and saving.
More warning time turns her **fear into a plan**, but she still expects to leave lettings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain or save.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while studying, and a rule that tenants can always reach a person.
